questions.q: Which request is the most polite?
options: I was wondering if you could send me the report.
questions.explain: Past continuous *I was wondering if…* is an indirect, very polite way to ask.
*How about / What about* + *-ing* makes a suggestion.

questions.q: On the phone: "Hello, *___* Maria. Can I speak to Tom?"
questions.explain: On the phone we identify ourselves with *It's…* or *This is…*.
*Half seven* is short for *half past seven*, 7.30.

questions.q: We arrived just *___* to catch the train.
questions.explain: *in time* = early enough to do something; *on time* = at the planned time.
Mountain ranges take *the*; single mountains, lakes and most countries don't.
*abroad* is an adverb and takes no preposition.
With a past reporting verb, the present usually moves back to the past.

questions.q: "Where do you live?" → He asked me where *___*.
questions.explain: Indirect questions use statement word order and no *do/did*.
Commands are reported with *tell / ask + object + to-infinitive*.
A positive sentence with *are* takes the negative tag *aren't you?*
The tag for *I am* is irregular: *aren't I?*
Agreeing with a positive present-simple statement: *So do I*.
After *hope* we use *so* (positive) or *not* (negative), never *it*.
Formal style prefers the passive and single-word verbs (*identify* rather than *find out*).

questions.q: In American English you say *___* the weekend.
questions.explain: British *at the weekend*, American *on the weekend*.

questions.q: *___* the forecast, it will be sunny.
questions.explain: *according to* + a source reports what it says (not for your own opinion).
*Actually* politely corrects a mistaken idea. It doesn't mean *currently*.

questions.q: It's high time you *___* a job.
questions.explain: *It's (high) time + subject + past simple* says something should already happen.

questions.q: Is there anything *___* I can do?
questions.explain: *else* follows indefinite words: *anything else, someone else*.
Irregular plurals not ending in *-s* add *'s*: *children's*.

options: My sister who lives in Rome, is a chef.
My sister, who lives in Rome, is a chef.
My sister, who lives in Rome is a chef.
My, sister who lives in Rome is a chef.
questions.explain: Non-defining relative clauses go between two commas.
The final consonant doubles when the last syllable is stressed: *be-GIN → beginning*.

questions.q: Which is a hedge that makes a statement less direct?
options: It might be a bit expensive.
questions.explain: Modals (*might*) and downtoners (*a bit*) soften what we say.

questions.q: I like sports *___* tennis and football.
questions.explain: *such as* introduces examples.
